AI servers: Dell reports a $132 billion order backlog and raises its forecast again, but Wall Street worries about margins after HPE's plunge

On Tuesday, November 24, Dell posted record results and raised its annual forecast for the third time, to $202 billion in revenue. But the day had been rough: its stock closed down nearly 12%, dragged lower by HPE, which plunged 16% after warning that its AI server margins would decline [1][2][5].
Dell now expects $202 billion in revenue for its fiscal year (ending in late January 2027), up from the $192 billion announced earlier, and adjusted earnings of $29.68 per share, up from $25.50 [1].
Sales of AI-optimized servers are expected to reach $78 billion for the year, up from the $74 billion forecast until now [1].
"We booked $60.2 billion in orders in the third quarter alone, bringing our AI backlog to an all-time record of $132.3 billion," said Jeff Clarke, chief operating officer [1].

Revenue for the quarter (August-October) reached about $54.9 billion, including $22 billion from AI servers, up 291% year on year [3][4]. For the next quarter, Dell is targeting $56.3 billion, above the expectations compiled by LSEG [3].
On Tuesday, Dell stock closed down nearly 12% before the release, then gained about 3% in after-hours trading [1].

The previous evening, Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) reported quarterly revenue up 50%, at $14.55 billion. But it forecasts an adjusted operating margin of 14% to 15% for the fiscal year ending in October 2027, down from 15.1% in 2026. Its stock lost about 16% [5].
Dell also warns that the margin of its server division will fall from 17% in the third quarter to just under 15% in the fourth [2].

Key takeaway: demand for AI servers is not slowing, but they earn less and less per unit sold. HPE's chief financial officer, Marie Myers, explains that costs are rising faster than selling prices [5].

So the stock market has changed its question: it no longer asks "how many servers?" but "at what margin?" [6]. This shift explains Dell's paradox: it beats expectations and raises its targets, yet its stock remains at about half its September record [14].

On Wednesday in Asia, the Seoul stock market fell by as much as 5.3% and Taiwan's by 5.1%, where many components for these servers are made, amid new threats of US tariffs [13]. Nvidia had fallen 5.9% on Tuesday, a day after a 31% jump [13].

You may not buy servers, but these figures show where AI money is going: $132 billion in pending orders at a single manufacturer. If you hold a global or US index fund, a large part of its performance depends on this theme.

How it works: the order backlog

The order backlog adds up orders that have been signed but not yet delivered. Dell only counts a sale in its revenue at the time of delivery. In the third quarter, the group received $60.2 billion in new AI orders and delivered $22 billion of AI servers [1][3]: so the backlog grew, to $132.3 billion [1], and was multiplied by more than seven in one year (+619%) according to Proactive Investors [11]. A large backlog promises future sales, but not profits: if chips and memory become more expensive between signing and delivery, the margin shrinks. That is exactly the concern that arose at HPE [5].

At the time, the market mostly wanted volume: each forecast increase sent the stock soaring.

After a quarter with $43.84 billion in sales (+88%), Dell raises its annual forecast to $165-169 billion, up from $138-142 billion, and targets about $60 billion in AI servers [9].
Targets were raised very quickly, which set the bar very high for the following quarters.

Another increase: $192 billion in expected annual sales, up from $167 billion, and $74 billion for AI servers, up from $60 billion [10].
In November, a third increase is no longer enough: the question of margins has taken over.

Peru: hundreds of informal gold miners surround Congress as they risk becoming illegal on December 31

On Tuesday, November 24, hundreds of artisanal miners gathered outside Congress in Lima. They are demanding another extension of Reinfo, the registry that protects them from prosecution and expires on December 31. Keiko Fujimori's government refuses and is pushing a new law, which Congress has not yet put on its agenda [1][2][3].
The rally, organized by Confemin, the national confederation of small-scale and artisanal miners, took place outside Congress and on Abancay Avenue, in central Lima [2][3].

Reinfo is a "formalization" registry: registered miners can work while waiting for their permits. The deadline expires on December 31; those left outside will then be considered illegal miners [1][2].

Demands vary: the EFE agency dispatch mentions a one-year extension, while Confemin is asking for four years and a national census of miners [2]. Other unions want a law extending Reinfo until 2030 and the resignation of the Minister of Energy and Mines [6][8].

The minister, Guillermo Shinno, warned on Tuesday that miners still without permits will become illegal if Congress does not pass the MAPE law on small-scale and artisanal mining by the end of December. According to him, this bill already gives them 18 more months [3].

Shinno believes the current system must change so that it no longer serves as cover for illegal mining operators [5]. Confemin, on the contrary, wants the future law to also include unregistered miners [5].

Two groups of artisanal miners have called for indefinite protests across the country, one since November 23, the other starting November 30; the government said it would not support another extension [4].

Key takeaway: the government wants to close a temporary registry that has been extended in the past, and miners who have not completed their paperwork risk losing their legal status all at once [2][3][7].

Last year, the government announced that Reinfo would end at the end of this year, with a simplified procedure pending the new law [2]. But the previous Parliament had already extended the registry under pressure from marches [7], and Confemin criticizes lawmakers for not putting the issue on the agenda of the Energy and Mines Committee [5]. No vote date has been set for the MAPE law [3].

The stakes are economic: gold and copper, Peru's top two exports, are driving the country's growth thanks to high prices [9]. The authorities accuse part of the informal mining sector of serving as a front for illegal gold mining [5].
For Keiko Fujimori, in power since July 28, the standoff comes at a bad time: her approval rating fell to 37% in November, according to an Ipsos poll, against 53% disapproval [10].

Some of the gold sold worldwide, including in jewelry bought in Europe, comes from informal mines in South America. This standoff will show whether Peru can better regulate the sector and separate good-faith small miners from illegal mining networks.

Colombia: a car bomb explodes outside the regional government headquarters in Villavicencio as the FARC dissidents' war reaches the cities

A car bomb exploded on the evening of Monday, November 23, outside the headquarters of the Meta department government in Villavicencio, a city of half a million people. At least 23 people were injured; no deaths have been reported. President Abelardo de la Espriella blames a FARC dissident group and vows "not to back down" [1][2][6].

The explosion occurred on Monday evening outside the offices of the Meta Gobernación, the regional government, in central Villavicencio [1]. An initial toll reported 12 injured, mostly security guards at the building [4].
On Tuesday, the authorities raised the toll to at least 23 injured, with no deaths [1][2]. The daily El Espectador counts 24 injured, including a 9-year-old girl [3].
According to the mayor, quoted by the website Colombia One, more than 85 buildings were damaged [5]. Prosecutors are trying to determine whether the rebel group FARC-EMC carried out the attack [1].

On X, conservative President Abelardo de la Espriella promised that the "narco-terrorists" would pay "for every drop of blood spilled and every building destroyed," and announced more operations against armed groups [1]. "We are not going to back down," he added [2].

He traveled to Villavicencio on Tuesday for a security council [5]. On Wednesday, he attributed the attack to a FARC dissident group and announced a reconstruction plan: 15 billion Colombian pesos to repair the Gobernación, the city center, housing and businesses, and a 40 billion peso zero-interest credit line for local entrepreneurs [6].

During the same night from Sunday to Monday, explosive-laden drones struck the police command in Cúcuta, on the Venezuelan border: three civilians were injured, including a baby, and more than 60 houses were hit; investigators suspect the ELN guerrilla group [7][8].
Key takeaway: violence by armed groups, long confined to the countryside, is now hitting regional capitals, at the heart of state power [1].

In Norte de Santander, the department of Cúcuta, the regional channel Canal TRO counts 62 drone attacks since the start of 2026, which have killed 20 people and injured 95 [10]. On November 12, a drone attack had already killed four soldiers in Tibú, in the same region [8].

The government has responded with more troops, bombings and military campaigns, but the attacks continue, notes the magazine Cambio [9]. The mayor of Villavicencio also suggests revenge by an armed group after military strikes [5].
For Abelardo de la Espriella, it is a test: he rejects any negotiation with "narco-terrorism" and is betting on force, a strategy that the repeated attacks are putting to the test [2][9].

If you are planning a trip to Colombia, this attack is a reminder that the threat no longer affects only rural areas: check your government's travel advice before you leave. For the economy, insecurity spreading to cities can slow foreign investment in the country.

news.2026-11-25-italie-meloni-maires-bud: Italy: after protests, Meloni urgently meets mayors and promises to consider more money for housing and transport
On Tuesday, November 24, Giorgia Meloni chaired an extraordinary meeting with mayors and provincial presidents at Palazzo Chigi in Rome, a day after protests against her 2027 budget [1][2].
The government said it was ready to "verify," during the budget's review in Parliament, possible additional funds for schools, local public transport and housing [1][3].

The president of the mayors' association (ANCI), Gaetano Manfredi, mayor of Naples, says he "found a response to our demands," but warns that municipalities cannot be burdened with "problems that are decades old" [2].
On the left, the daily Il Manifesto sees only "a few vague promises and zero additional resources" [4].
The €26 billion budget had already triggered a general strike by the CGIL union on November 20, with tens of thousands of protesters [5].
Key takeaway: under pressure from the streets and the cities, Meloni leaves the door ajar without putting a figure on anything [1][4].
Lawmakers have until Thursday, November 26, at 2 p.m. to file up to 700 amendments in committee; the bill will reach the floor on December 18 [6].
If you travel to Italy this winter, more transport strikes remain possible as long as the budget has not been passed.

news.2026-11-25-indonesie-complot-prabow: Indonesia: two counterterrorism chiefs dismissed over an alleged plot against Prabowo, who is seeking a new vice president

On Tuesday, November 24, the Indonesian police dismissed two senior officers from its counterterrorism unit, Densus 88, accused of spying on government members in a case involving an alleged plot against President Prabowo Subianto [1].

Brigadier General Muhammad Tedjo Kusumo and Guntur Yayus Putra "monitored and tailed" people with no link to counterterrorism, "in fact government officials," according to police spokesperson Trunoyudo Wisnu Andika; both will appeal [1].

The wiretapping case broke in October; six suspects have been named, including former national police chief Listyo Sigit Prabowo, who was removed on November 4 from his post as head of the presidential cabinet [2].
Two other police officers had already been dismissed on November 10 and 17 [2].
Key takeaway: Indonesia is going through a crisis at the top of the state, between suspicions of espionage and a vacant vice presidency [1][3].

On Monday, November 23, Prabowo proposed two ministers to Parliament, Andi Amran Sulaiman (Agriculture) and Sugiono (former foreign minister), to replace Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka, who resigned this month [3][4].
If you follow Southeast Asia for travel or savings, the December 2 election will show whether Jakarta quickly gets a full executive back.

news.2026-11-25-arabie-saoudite-budget-2: Saudi Arabia: under Houthi missile fire, Riyadh approves a $371 billion 2027 budget with a $51 billion deficit

On Tuesday, November 24, at a session chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the Saudi government adopted a 2027 budget that projects 1,392 billion riyals in spending against 1,202 billion in revenue, a deficit of about 190 billion riyals [1][2][3].
In dollars: $371 billion in spending, $320 billion in revenue and a $51 billion gap [1][3].

The deficit is expected to narrow to 3.6% of GDP, down from an estimated 4.9% in 2026, or 245 billion riyals, far more than the 165 billion forecast a year ago, because the war disrupted oil exports [2].
The Finance Ministry forecasts the economy will contract by 2.1% in 2026, then rebound by 10.9% in 2027 [4].
Public debt is set to climb to 1,923 billion riyals by the end of 2027, or 35.9% of GDP, financed by bonds, sukuk (Islamic bonds) and loans [1][3].
Key takeaway: despite a year of war, the kingdom keeps spending more than it earns, and fills the gap by borrowing [1][2].
The budget is adopted as Yemen's Houthi rebels step up missile and drone fire on the country, and as non-oil growth slows [2][3].
